# ECON 0100 | Homework C1 | Externalities

*Due: Friday, Oct. 16*

Homework is designed to both test your knowledge and challenge you to apply familiar concepts in new applications. Answer clearly and completely, and show your work so you can later understand your thought process. You are welcomed and encouraged to work in groups as long as your work is your own. Submit your answers on Gradescope when you’re finished: each answer there is a selection.

## Q1 | Malodorous Byproducts

Butterbeer is beloved by Hogwarts students and teachers alike and is widely available at wizarding shops. But the beverage has the negative effect of generating displeasing odors from its imbibers. Model the private market for butterbeer using private and social cost and benefit curves. Indicate on your graph the private equilibrium quantity and social equilibrium quantity.

Preferences for butterbeer and its marginal cost can be represented by the following relationships.

$$
D: P_B = 40 - Q_D \qquad\qquad S: P_S = 10 + \frac{1}{2} Q_S
$$

Prices are in galleons and quantity is in bottles. The odor imposes a cost of 9 galleons per bottle on everyone nearby.

## Q2 | Dragon Pox

Dragon Pox is spreading through the wizarding world. A dose of Gorsemoor’s Draught keeps a witch or wizard from catching it, so whoever drinks it also can’t pass Dragon Pox on to anyone else. Let’s model the market for the draught and assume the following.

1. There is a linear marginal private benefit curve for the draught.
2. The draught carries with it a positive externality.
3. There is a linear upward sloping supply curve for the draught. ~~The supply curve for the vaccine is a little funny, and we’ll talk about imperfect close substitutes in the next few weeks. But we’ll just assume it’s there.~~

Use a graph to discuss the welfare in the market and any potential market failure.

The graph below shows the market, with prices in galleons and quantity in doses. The upper downward-sloping curve is marginal social benefit and the lower one is marginal private benefit. Supply is both the private and the social cost. The lettered regions are for the questions.

![Market for Gorsemoor’s Draught with MPB, MSB and S, and regions A, B and C](data:image/svg+xml;base64,) 

Market Quantity: \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ Socially Efficient Quantity: \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

Deadweight Loss region (letter): \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

Why does the market provide too few doses?

> a\) Each dose costs society more to brew than it costs the seller.
>
> b\) Each dose is worth more to society than to the witch or wizard buying it, so at the market quantity marginal social benefit is still above marginal cost.
>
> c\) Buyers value each dose less than sellers’ marginal cost, so too few buyers enter the market.
>
> d\) The market quantity is already socially efficient, so no doses are missing.

## Q3 | Deadweight Loss Intuition

Which of the following best explains the intuition behind the deadweight loss associated with a negative externality like the one in Q1?

> a\) The externality causes the market to produce too much of the good, leading to a surplus and reduced consumer surplus.
>
> b\) The externality causes the market to produce too little of the good, leading to a shortage and reduced producer surplus.
>
> c\) The externality causes the market to produce at a quantity where the marginal social cost of production exceeds the marginal social benefit of consumption, leading to inefficiency and reduced total surplus.
>
> d\) The externality causes the market to produce at a quantity where the marginal social benefit of consumption exceeds the marginal social cost of production, leading to inefficiency and reduced total surplus.

If the marginal cost of a gallon of gas is \$4.00, the negative externality is \$2.50, and the marginal benefit is \$4.50, what is the deadweight loss?

Deadweight Loss: \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_
